description: We’re curious builders interested in space, technology, coding, data, and design. We turn ideas into working projects and value creativity, different perspectives, and initiative. Looking for developers, AI/ML enthusiasts, researchers, designers, and communicators. Got skills and ideas? Join us and let’s build something awesome together!
summary:
TerraMirror is a geospatial exploration platform developed to identify Earth locations that resemble selected lunar and Martian environments. It brings together three planetary map experiences: an Earth Offline Atlas, NASA lunar imagery and terrain references from LRO/LOLA, and Martian topography from MOLA/HRSC.

The platform enables users to explore predefined candidate locations, analyse custom coordinates, perform regional terrain scans, and compare geographical characteristics using elevation, slope, relief and surface roughness metrics. It also incorporates NASA POWER climate data for independent environmental screening and supports supplementary georeferenced elevation datasets from partner space agencies, including ISRO, ESA and JAXA.

TerraMirror addresses the challenge by making planetary analogue exploration more accessible through an integrated geospatial research workflow. By connecting terrestrial geography with open space-agency data, it provides a foundation for studying potential Earth analogues of extraterrestrial environments and supporting future planetary exploration research.
details:
TerraMirror is a project we developed to explore whether places on Earth share similarities with certain regions of the Moon and Mars. The idea came from a simple question: if we want to understand and prepare for exploring other worlds, can we start by studying similar environments on our own planet?

We built a platform that brings together three different map experiences: an Earth Atlas, a lunar map using NASA LRO/LOLA data, and a Mars map using MOLA/HRSC references. Users can explore different locations, select potential analogue sites, analyse custom coordinates and compare terrain characteristics such as elevation, slope, surface variation and roughness. We also use NASA POWER data to examine climate conditions separately.

One of the main things we wanted was to bring different sources of geographical and space-agency data into one place instead of making users explore them individually. We have also added support for supplementary datasets from ISRO, ESA and JAXA, which can be imported for additional terrain analysis.

We developed TerraMirror using HTML, CSS, JavaScript and Python, along with tools and libraries such as FastAPI, NumPy, SciPy and Rasterio.

What makes the project interesting is the connection it creates between Earth and planetary exploration. We wanted to make the process of finding and comparing analogue environments more visual and accessible, while keeping the scientific limitations clear. Factors such as data availability, terrain resolution, coordinate accuracy and measurement differences were important considerations during development.

TerraMirror is still an exploratory prototype, but we hope it can become a useful starting point for students and researchers interested in planetary science and future Moon and Mars exploration.
